mainTopic: The son of uncertain priestly father (striking, cursing, and serving with the משמרות), then the start of פרק מצות חליצה: the court and the shoe for חליצה
overview: This amud finishes the case of a son whose father could be either of two men, both of them כהנים. A ברייתא debates whether he is liable for hitting or cursing them. The גמרא settles two different reports of רבי יהודה's view by saying two תנאים passed it down differently. רבי חנינא explains the exemption: cursing a parent is compared to cursing ה׳, so it applies only to one clear father with no 'partnership', and striking follows cursing. Next, the גמרא shows that the son must go up with both fathers' משמרות even against his will, because of פגם משפחה, the family's good name. רב פפא then explains that the son gets a share only when both fathers are in the same משמר and the same בית אב. After the הדרן closing פרק נושאין על האנוסה, a new פרק opens with a משנה about חליצה: who must be present, and which shoes count. The גמרא learns that the three judges must at least be able to read out the פסוקים. It then shows how the תנא קמא gets three judges and רבי יהודה gets five from the פסוקים. It ends partway through a proof of where רבי יהודה learns that ordinary people may serve, and that proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: both possible fathers are כהנים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the opening words of the משנה's case where both possible fathers are כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If both of them were כהנים, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pointing back to a line in the משנה so it can discuss it. This is a setup line that opens the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a son whose father could be either of two men, and here both of them are כהנים. The 'etc.' tells us the גמרא wants us to remember the rest of that משנה, which deals with striking and cursing these two men.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them were כהנים (both possible fathers)
Etc.; the rest of the quote is assumed

phrases.english: If both of them were priests, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Both of them' means the two men who could each be the boy's father.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion of this line in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case under discussion: a son of uncertain father where both possible fathers are כהנים.

steps.title: The ברייתא: he is liable in every case
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that the son is liable for striking or cursing the two possible fathers, whether one after the other or at the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If he hit this one and then hit that one, or cursed this one and then cursed that one, or cursed both at once, or hit both at once, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that discusses striking and cursing the two possible fathers. The first opinion says he is liable in all four ways it lists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is simple: one of these two men is definitely his father. So if he hit or cursed both of them, he surely hit or cursed his real father, whether he did it one at a time or together.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; introduces a ברייתא
At the same time, in one act

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If he struck this one and then struck that one,
or cursed this one and then cursed that one,
or cursed both of them at the same time,
or struck both of them at the same time —
he is liable.
phrases.notes: Liable for the death penalty for striking or cursing a parent, since one of them is surely his father.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that rules on the משנה's case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, the son is liable for striking or cursing both possible fathers, whether one after the other or at once.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: liable together, exempt one after the other
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה disagrees: at the same time he is liable, but one after the other he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: If he did it to both at once, he is liable. If he did it one after the other, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: Within the same ברייתא, רבי יהודה gives a different opinion. He only holds the son liable when he hits or curses both men in one act.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When it happens in one act, that single act surely hit or cursed his real father. When it happens one after the other, each act on its own is doubtful, since any single man might not be his father. That is why רבי יהודה exempts him in that case.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
At the same time — he is liable,
one after the other — he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the תנא קמא in the case of one after the other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: liable only if done to both in one act; exempt if done one after the other.

steps.title: A different ברייתא quotes רבי יהודה as exempting even at once
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points to another ברייתא in which רבי יהודה exempts the son even when he does it at the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in another ברייתא: רבי יהודה says he is exempt even at the same time!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the version of רבי יהודה we just learned. Another ברייתא reports his view the opposite way for the case of 'at the same time'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 3, רבי יהודה said 'at the same time = liable'. Here a different ברייתא quotes him as saying 'at the same time = exempt'. So which is רבי יהודה's real opinion?

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught (in a ברייתא); introduces a contradiction

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: Rabbi Yehuda says:
He is exempt even at the same time!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contradicts the version of רבי יהודה given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The report in step 3 that רבי יהודה holds him liable when it is done at the same time.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two ברייתות quote רבי יהודה with opposite rulings for the same case.

steps.title: Two תנאים report רבי יהודה differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that two different תנאים passed down רבי יהודה's view in two different ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are two תנאים, each reporting what רבי יהודה held.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying both ברייתות are real. They come from two תנאים who disagree about what רבי יהודה said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not try to fit the two sources together. It simply accepts that there were two traditions about רבי יהודה's opinion. One says he exempts only one after the other, and the other says he exempts even at the same time.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a dispute about the law between רבי יהודה and someone else. It is a dispute about what רבי יהודה himself said.

phrases.english: These are two tanna'im, each reporting the view of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributes the conflicting sources to two different traditions about the same Tanna.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought there was one fixed opinion of רבי יהודה, so the two ברייתות contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two תנאים hold different versions of רבי יהודה's view, so there is no contradiction.

steps.title: Why exempt him at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reasoning of the opinion that exempts the son.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the one who exempts him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind the opinion that exempts the son, even though one of the two men is surely his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is puzzling, because he definitely struck or cursed his father, either in one act or across two acts. The גמרא wants to know why the Torah would not punish him.

phrases.english: What is the reasoning of the one who exempts?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the exempting view just mentioned.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for exempting a son of uncertain father from striking or cursing.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: no liability where there is 'partnership'
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא links cursing a parent to cursing ה׳. Just as ה׳ has no partner, the curse of a parent applies only when there is no doubt about who the father is. Striking is then linked to cursing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: 'Blessing' (meaning cursing) is said below, about parents, and above, about ה׳. Just as the one above has no partnership, so too the one below must have no partnership. And striking is compared to cursing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא gives a source from the פסוקים for the exemption. He also extends the same rule from cursing to striking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's word for cursing appears both for cursing a parent and for cursing ה׳, so the two are learned from each other. Cursing ה׳ involves only One, with no 'partner'. So cursing a parent is only punished when the father is one clear person, not when two men 'share' the doubt. Since the Torah puts striking and cursing side by side, the same exemption applies to striking.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'blessing'; here a polite way of saying 'curse'
Below / above (later and earlier in the Torah, or parent and ה׳)
Partnership; here, two possible fathers sharing the role
Was compared (a היקש, a link drawn between two topics)

steps.whatToRemember: The exempting view is based on רבי חנינא's comparison: liability for cursing (and striking) a parent requires a definite, single father, just as cursing ה׳ involves no 'partnership'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key principle: Torah punishment for harming a parent depends on a clearly identified parent, not just the knowledge that one of two people is the parent.

phrases.english: Rabbi Hanina said:
'Blessing' is stated below,
phrases.notes: 'Blessing' is a polite way of saying 'curse'. 'Below' is the פסוק about cursing a parent, ויקרא 20:9.

phrases.english: and 'blessing' is stated above.
phrases.notes: 'Above' is the פסוק about cursing ה׳‎, שמות 22:27.

phrases.english: Just as above, where there is no partnership —
so too below, only where there is no partnership.
phrases.notes: No 'partnership' means the father is one clear person, not one of two men.

phrases.english: And striking is compared to cursing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: נֶאֶמְרָה בְּרָכָה לְמַטָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: By comparing cursing a parent to cursing ה׳, liability needs a single, certain father; striking follows cursing through the היקש.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: he goes up with his משמר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: the son goes up to serve with the משמר of each possible father.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And he goes up with his משמר, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה about Temple service. This is a setup line that prepares the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The כהנים were divided into משמרות, groups that served in the מקדש in turns. Since this son could belong to either father's group, he goes up with both. The 'etc.' recalls the rest of the line: he does not receive a share.

keyTerms.meaning: He goes up (to serve in the מקדש)
A priestly watch, a group of כהנים serving in rotation

phrases.english: And he goes up with his watch, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son goes up with the משמר of each possible father but does not receive a share.

steps.title: Why go up if he gets no share?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the son would go up to serve if he gets no portion.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he does not get a share, why does he go up?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the point is of going up to serve when he gets nothing from the offerings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a כהן who serves gets a portion of the offerings. If this son gets nothing, the גמרא wonders why the משנה says he goes up at all.

phrases.english: But since he does not take a share,
why does he go up?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּאֵינוֹ חוֹלֵק, לָמָּה עוֹלֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the ruling quoted in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What purpose there is in going up to serve without receiving a share.

steps.title: Rejecting the question: he wants to do a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects its own question: obviously he goes up because he wants to do a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does he go up?! He says, 'I want to do a מצוה!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the question it just asked. A person serves in the מקדש for the מצוה, not just for the portion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed the only reason to serve is to get a share. But serving is itself a מצוה, so wanting to go up makes perfect sense. That means the question as asked does not work.

phrases.english: Why does he go up?!
Doesn't he say: I want to do a מצוה!

steps.triggerLanguage: לָמָּה עוֹלֶה?! הָאָמַר: בָּעֵינָא דְּנֶיעְבֵּיד מִצְוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the question of step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The question of step 9 as a whole.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed the only reason to serve is to receive a share, ignoring the desire to do a מצוה.

steps.title: 'He goes up' means he must go up, even against his will
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reworks the question: the משנה says 'goes up', not 'went up', which teaches that he is required to go up even against his will.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the משנה does not say 'he went up'. It says 'he goes up', meaning even against his will.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what its question was really about. The משנה's wording shows that the son is obligated to go up, so the real question is why he would be forced to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה had said 'went up' (עלה), it would only mean he may go up if he wants. 'Goes up' (עולה) sounds like a requirement: he goes up even if he does not want to. A desire to do a מצוה explains why he might choose to go, but not why he would be forced to go.

keyTerms.meaning: He went up (past tense; describes something done by choice)

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's present-tense 'עולה' teaches that the son of uncertain priestly father must go up with both משמרות, even against his will, even though he receives no share.
steps.confusionAlert: The point is not that he may go up for the מצוה. That was already obvious. The point is that the wording makes going up an obligation.

phrases.english: Rather: it does not state 'he went up,'
but rather 'he goes up' —
against his will.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reshapes the question after the rejection in step 10, based on the משנה's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of the משנה's wording (present tense signals obligation).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was why he would want to go up at all, and the answer 'for the מצוה' seemed to end it.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'עולה' means he must go up even against his will, so the question is really about why he is obligated, which the wish to do a מצוה cannot explain.

steps.title: He must serve because of the family's reputation
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoted through a chain of teachers, explains that the son is forced to go up and serve because of פגם משפחה, possible damage to the family name.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר חנינא said that אביי said that רבי אסי said that רבי יוחנן said: He must go up because of a flaw to the family.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains why the son must go up to serve even if he doesn't want to: to protect the family's reputation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 showed from the word 'goes up' that the son is required to serve. This step gives the reason behind that requirement. If he stayed away, it could hurt the name of the families he comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: A flaw or stain on the family's name

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that his duty to serve is not about getting portions. It is about protecting the status of the כהונה families.

phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Chanina said
that Abaye said that Rabbi Asi said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Because of a flaw to the family.
phrases.notes: If he never showed up to serve, people might think the families he comes from are not fit for כהונה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the requirement established in step 11
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the son required to go up and serve, even against his will?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because of פגם משפחה: if he does not serve, the families' name would be harmed.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: both fathers in one משמר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next clause of the משנה: if both possible fathers were in the same משמר, the son gets one share.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: And if both of them were in one משמר, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. This sets up a question about that line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the משנה taught that when the fathers were in two different משמרות, the son gets no share. Now it says that if both were in one משמר, he takes one share. The גמרא is about to ask what the difference is.

keyTerms.meaning: A priestly watch; one of the groups of כהנים who served in the מקדש in turn
Etc.; the rest of the quote is understood

phrases.english: And if both of them were
in one watch, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If both possible fathers belong to one משמר, the son receives one share.

steps.title: Why should one משמר be different from two?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה. With two משמרות, each group pushes him away. With one משמר, each בית אב could push him away in the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about two watches, where he gets no share? There, he goes to this watch and they push him away, and he goes to that watch and they push him away. With one watch too, he goes to this family house and they push him away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the son gets a share when both fathers are in one משמר. The same problem that stopped him with two משמרות should apply here too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two משמרות, each group can say 'you belong to the other one,' so he gets nothing. A single משמר is also split into smaller family groups, each called a בית אב, and each serves on its own day. So each בית אב could also say 'you belong to the other one.'

keyTerms.meaning: A family group within a משמר that served on a set day

phrases.english: What is different about two watches, that he does not get a share?
Because he goes to this watch and they push him away,
phrases.notes: They tell him, 'You might belong to the other watch, so go take your share there.'

phrases.english: and he goes to that watch and they push him away.
With one watch too:

phrases.aramaic: אָזֵיל לְהַאי בֵּית אָב וּמְדַחוּ לֵיהּ!
phrases.english: he goes to this family house and they push him away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה clause quoted in step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the son gets one share when both fathers are in one משמר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason he is turned away with two משמרות also applies to two בתי אב within one משמר, so he should get nothing there too.

steps.title: רב פפא: same משמר and same בית אב
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the משנה means both fathers were in the same משמר and the same בית אב. Then no group can push him away, and he takes one share.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This is what the משנה means: If both of them were in one watch and one family house, he takes one share.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by reading the משנה more narrowly. The fathers were not just in one משמר but also in one בית אב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both possible fathers are in the same בית אב, it doesn't matter which one is really his father. Either way he belongs to that group, so nobody can send him elsewhere. That is why he gets a share.
steps.whatToRemember: The son of uncertain fatherhood gets a share only when both possible fathers are in the same משמר and the same בית אב. Otherwise each group can push him away, though he still must serve because of פגם משפחה.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: This is what it is saying:
If both of them were one watch
and one family house
he takes one share.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case in the משנה (הכי קאמר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to give a share whenever both fathers were in one משמר, even in different בתי אב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is talking about fathers in the same משמר and the same בית אב, so no group can turn him away.

steps.title: הדרן: closing פרק נושאין על האנוסה
steps.stepSummary: The traditional closing line for the פרק נושאין על האנוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק נושאין על האנוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the פרק. It is not part of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying הדרן expresses a hope to come back and learn this פרק again. A new פרק begins after this line.

keyTerms.meaning: The name of the פרק that is ending

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'One may marry a woman who was raped'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק after the final discussion
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק נושאין על האנוסה is complete.

steps.title: New משנה: three judges, and which shoes work for חליצה
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה says חליצה is done before three judges, even if they are הדיוטות. A regular shoe or a sandal with a heel is valid. A soft אנפיליא or a sandal without a heel is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The מצוה of חליצה is done before three judges, even if all three are laymen. If she did חליצה with a shoe, it is valid. With a soft felt shoe, it is invalid. A sandal with a heel is valid. One without a heel is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק begins with a new משנה about how חליצה is done. First it sets out who must be present and what kind of footwear counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives two rules here. First, the court of three does not have to be expert judges. Second, the shoe must be real, sturdy footwear: a regular shoe or a sandal with a heel counts, while a soft felt shoe or a heelless sandal does not.

keyTerms.meaning: The ceremony where the widow removes the shoe of her dead husband's brother, freeing her from יבום
Laymen, people who are not trained judges
A soft felt or cloth shoe without a hard sole

phrases.english: The מצוה of chalitza is done before three judges,
and even if all three of them are laymen.
If she did chalitza with a shoe, her chalitza is valid;
with a soft felt shoe, her chalitza is invalid.
With a sandal that has a heel, it is valid,
and with one that has no heel, it is invalid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new פרק and topic right after the closing line of the previous פרק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חליצה is done before three judges, even laymen. A regular shoe or a sandal with a heel is valid. A soft felt shoe or a heelless sandal is invalid.

steps.title: משנה continued: where the shoe sits and unusual shoes
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues. A shoe on the leg below the knee works, but above the knee does not. A borrowed sandal, a wooden sandal, a left shoe on the right foot, a big shoe he can walk in, or a small shoe covering most of the foot are all valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the shoe is on the leg from the knee down, the חליצה is valid. From the knee up, it is invalid. A sandal that isn't his, a wooden sandal, or a left shoe on the right foot are all valid. A shoe too big that he can still walk in, or too small but covering most of his foot, is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה keeps listing cases. Now it covers where on the leg the shoe can be, and odd shoes that still count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line at the knee sets the limit for what counts as the 'foot' area for חליצה. The other cases show that the shoe doesn't need to be his own, made of leather, or a perfect fit. It only needs to work as a shoe he can walk in or one that covers most of the foot.
steps.whatToRemember: The shoe for חליצה must be real, usable footwear. It does not have to belong to him, be leather, be on the correct foot, or fit perfectly.

phrases.english: From the knee and below, it is a valid chalitza.
phrases.notes: This is talking about where the shoe sits, for example on the stump of a leg that was cut off below the knee.

phrases.english: From the knee and above, it is an invalid chalitza.
If she did chalitza with a sandal that is not his,
or with a sandal made of wood,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בְּשֶׁל שְׂמֹאל בְּיָמִין — חֲלִיצָה כְּשֵׁרָה.
phrases.english: or with a left shoe worn on the right foot, it is a valid chalitza.

phrases.aramaic: חָלְצָה בְּגָדוֹל שֶׁהוּא יָכוֹל לַהֲלוֹךְ בּוֹ,
phrases.english: If she did chalitza with a big shoe that he is able to walk in,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בְּקָטָן שֶׁהוּא חוֹפֶה אֶת רוֹב רַגְלוֹ — חֲלִיצָתָהּ כְּשֵׁרָה.
phrases.english: or with a small one that covers most of his foot, her chalitza is valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with more shoe cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Below the knee is valid and above the knee is invalid. A borrowed shoe, a wooden one, one on the wrong foot, or a poorly fitting but usable shoe are all valid.

steps.title: Why does the משנה say 'judges' if laymen are fine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if even three הדיוטות are allowed, why did the משנה bother calling them דיינים?
steps.simpleTranslation: Since even three laymen are enough, why do I need the word 'judges'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts on the משנה and points out a wording problem. The word 'judges' seems useless if laymen are allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה seems to contradict itself. It says 'three judges' but then says even laymen are fine. So the word 'judges' looks unnecessary, and the גמרא wants to know what it adds.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (asking why a word is needed)

phrases.english: GEMARA: And since even three laymen are fine,
why do I need it to say 'judges'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמֵאַחַר דַּאֲפִילּוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה הֶדְיוֹטוֹת, דַּיָּינִין לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions a word in the opening line of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If laymen are allowed, calling them judges seems unneeded.

steps.title: They must at least be able to read out the פסוקים like judges
steps.stepSummary: The word 'judges' teaches that the three must at least know how to read out the פסוקים of חליצה for the people doing it, the way judges would.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us that we need three people who know how to read out the words, like judges.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The word 'judges' adds a basic requirement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They don't need to be real judges. But they cannot be people who can't read. They must be able to read the פסוקים aloud so the יבם and יבמה can repeat them, like judges do.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
To read the words out for others to repeat

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
that we need three people who know how to read out the words
like judges.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the word 'judges'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains what the extra word teaches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'judges' seemed to add nothing once laymen are allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The laymen must at least be able to read out the פסוקים like judges.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the same thing, and רבי יהודה requires five
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that our משנה matches a ברייתא that says three who can read out the words like judges. In that ברייתא, רבי יהודה says five are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have learned in our משנה what the רבנן taught: the מצוה of חליצה is done before three people who know how to read out the words like judges. רבי יהודה says: before five.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the answer it just gave is also found in a ברייתא. The ברייתא also brings in a new opinion, רבי יהודה, who wants five.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spells out the exact rule the גמרא found inside the word 'judges'. It also adds an argument: the תנא קמא says three, while רבי יהודה says five. This sets up the next question about where each number comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: We have already learned this (in our משנה)
A תנא who disagrees here and requires five

phrases.english: We have learned in our mishna what the Sages taught:
The מצוה of chalitza is done before three
who know how to read out the words like judges.
Rabbi Yehuda says: before five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links the answer in step 20 to a ברייתא and brings in רבי יהודה's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא: three who can read out the words like judges. רבי יהודה: five.

steps.title: What is the source for the תנא קמא's three?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the תנא קמא requires three.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the תנא קמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks for the source of each side's number, starting with the תנא קמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that there is an argument between three and five, the גמרא wants to see how each number comes from the פסוקים.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: What is the reason of the first tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the תנא קמא's number from step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where the number three comes from

steps.title: זקנים means two, and a court can't be even, so three
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that the word זקנים means at least two. A בית דין may not have an even number, so one is added, making three.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'Elders' means two. A court may not be even-numbered, so we add one more. That makes three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא that shows how the תנא קמא gets the number three.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plural word like זקנים means at least two people. Two judges could split one against one, so a בית דין must be an odd number. Adding one gives three.

keyTerms.meaning: A court with an even number of judges, which could split evenly

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'Elders' means two,
and a court may not have an even number,
so we add one more to them;
so here there are three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: זקנים means two, and an odd-numbered court adds one more, making three.

steps.title: רבי יהודה counts two words, so five
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה counts both זקני and זקנים, two each, which makes four. Since a court can't be even, he adds one to make five.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה: 'Elders of' means two, and 'Elders' means two more. A court may not be even-numbered, so we add one more. That makes five.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now shows how רבי יהודה reaches five from the same kind of reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה uses two words in the פסוקים, each worth two, which makes four. Four is even, so one is added to make five. The two sides use the same 'no even court' rule. They argue only about how many words to count.
steps.whatToRemember: Both the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה agree a court may not be even-numbered. The תנא קמא counts one word, which gives three. רבי יהודה counts two words, which gives five.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda: 'Elders of' means two,
'Elders' means two more,
and a court may not have an even number,
so we add one more to them;
so here there are five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יהודה's source, alongside the תנא קמא's source in step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two words each mean two, which makes four. One is added to avoid an even court, which makes five.

steps.title: What does the תנא קמא do with the word זקני?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the תנא קמא uses the word זקני, since he did not use it to count judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא קמא, what does he do with this word זקני?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that the תנא קמא counted only the word זקנים to reach three judges. It asks what he does with the other word, זקני.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה used both זקני and זקנים to reach five. The תנא קמא used only זקנים. Every word in the תורה should teach something, so the גמרא wants to know what זקני teaches according to the תנא קמא.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in the ברייתא
'The elders of', a word in the חליצה פסוק
What does he do with it? (How does he use this word?)

phrases.english: And the first Tanna,
what does he do with this word "elders of"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא קַמָּא, הַאי זִקְנֵי מַאי עָבֵיד לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After seeing רבי יהודה count both words, the גמרא asks how the תנא קמא uses the word he did not count.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The purpose of the word זקני according to the תנא קמא.

steps.title: זקני includes even three ordinary people
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא uses זקני to teach that even three ordinary people can serve as the court for חליצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs it to include even three ordinary people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the תנא קמא uses זקני to teach that the three judges do not have to be experts. Even ordinary people are allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the תנא קמא gets two separate lessons from the פסוק. זקנים gives the number three, and זקני teaches that ordinary people count. Earlier, step 20 showed they still must be able to read out the פסוקים.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it (for a different lesson)
Ordinary people who are not expert, ordained judges

phrases.english: He needs it to include
even three ordinary people.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְרַבּוֹיֵי אֲפִילּוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה הֶדְיוֹטוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to the תנא קמא, זקני teaches that even three ordinary people are allowed to serve.

steps.title: Where does רבי יהודה learn that ordinary people are allowed?
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי יהודה used זקני for counting, the גמרא asks where he learns that ordinary people are allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה, where does he learn that ordinary people are allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבי יהודה. He already used זקני to count judges, so where does he learn that ordinary people can serve?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא learned the rule about ordinary people from זקני. רבי יהודה used up that word to reach five judges, so he needs a different source for the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who holds that five judges are needed for חליצה
From where does he know it?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda,
from where does he know that ordinary people are allowed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 25: now the גמרא asks the same kind of question about רבי יהודה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי יהודה's source that ordinary people may serve for חליצה.

steps.title: He learns it from the word לעיני
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה learns it from לעיני ('before the eyes of'), which rules out blind people.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from 'before the eyes of', as the Master said: 'before the eyes of' excludes blind people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says רבי יהודה's source is the word לעיני. It quotes a teaching that this word rules out blind people from serving.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first glance, a rule about blind people says nothing about ordinary people. The גמרא is setting up the next step, which explains how ruling out blind people proves that ordinary people are allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Before the eyes of', a word in the חליצה פסוק
The Master said (quoting an earlier teaching)

phrases.english: He derives it from "before the eyes of",
as the Master said:
"Before the eyes of" excludes blind people,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה learns it from לעיני, which rules out blind people.

steps.title: Ruling out blind people proves ordinary people are allowed
steps.stepSummary: Since the תורה needed a word to rule out blind people, ordinary people must be allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since 'before the eyes of' was needed to exclude blind people, learn from this that even ordinary people are allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the proof. The fact that the תורה had to rule out blind people shows that ordinary people are allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof works by asking why the word is needed. If the court had to be expert judges, blind people would already be ruled out, and the word would be extra. The next step spells this out.

phrases.english: And since "before the eyes of" was necessary
to exclude blind people,
learn from this that even ordinary people are allowed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִדְּאִיצְטְרִיךְ לְעֵינֵי לְמַעוֹטֵי סוֹמִים, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the source in step 28 proves the rule about ordinary people.
steps.raayaObject: According to רבי יהודה, ordinary people may serve as the court for חליצה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word לעיני, which was needed to exclude blind people.

steps.title: If experts were needed, why rule out the blind?
steps.stepSummary: If סנהדרין-level judges were required, there would be no reason for a פסוק to rule out blind people.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you thought we need judges fit for the סנהדרין, why would I need a word to exclude blind people?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the logic of the proof. If the judges had to be fit for the סנהדרין, the word ruling out blind people would be unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that judges fit for the סנהדרין already cannot be blind. So the extra word only adds something if the court is made of ordinary people, who could otherwise include a blind person.

keyTerms.meaning: If it enters your mind (if you were to think)
The high court of expert judges

phrases.english: For if it enters your mind
that we need judges fit for the Sanhedrin,
why do I need a word to exclude blind people?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the inference in step 29 works.
steps.raayaObject: The word לעיני would be extra if expert judges were required.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rule that סנהדרין judges must be free of physical defects, brought in the next step.

steps.title: רב יוסף: a court must be free of any defect
steps.stepSummary: Blind people are already ruled out from expert courts by רב יוסף's teaching that a court must be free of any physical defect.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is already learned from what רב יוסף taught, as רב יוסף taught: Just as a court is clean in righteousness, so too a court is clean of any physical defect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב יוסף's ברייתא to show that a proper court already cannot have blind judges. This is why the word לעיני must be teaching about ordinary people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף compares a court's honesty to its judges' bodies: both must be complete. If that rule already rules out blind experts, then לעיני must be needed for a court of ordinary people. That proves ordinary people are allowed for חליצה.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who taught this ברייתא
Clean in righteousness: honest and free of suspicion

steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא learns that ordinary people may serve from זקני. רבי יהודה learns it from לעיני, which would be extra if expert judges were needed, since experts already cannot be blind.

phrases.english: That is already derived from what Rav Yosef taught,
as Rav Yosef taught:
Just as a court is clean in righteousness,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ בֵּית דִּין מְנוּקִּים מִכׇּל מוּם,
phrases.english: so too a court is clean of any physical defect,

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּתָנֵי רַב יוֹסֵף נָפְקָא, דְּתָנֵי רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind the claim in step 30 that experts cannot be blind anyway.
steps.raayaObject: A court of expert judges already cannot include blind people.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יוסף's ברייתא: a court must be clean of any physical defect, just as it is clean in righteousness.
